tagline: High meadows and a log cabin above an eroding amphitheater.
intro: The Cedar Breaks scenic drive links SR-143 and SR-14 through high meadows and Dixie National Forest. The drive ranges from 9,900 to 10,500 feet in elevation, with a 4 percent grade. Iron oxides give the amphitheater’s rocks red, orange and yellow colors; manganese oxides add purple. SR-148 has both Utah Scenic Byway and National Forest Scenic Byway designations. Utah’s tourism office highlights views into an amphitheater more than 2,000 feet deep and three miles across.

The state highway designation began in 1927 as SR-55, connecting SR-14 to the southern monument boundary. It became part of SR-143 in 1969, but the monument road was excluded from that number, leaving two disconnected state highway sections. The southern section became SR-148 in 1985; the National Forest Scenic Byway designation followed in 1991.

For a north-to-south trip, join the monument road from SR-143 near North View. Continue toward the Alpine Pond trailhead at Chessman Ridge and the rim visitor-center area at Point Supreme. The road generally closes from mid-November through late May, when it becomes a groomed route for snowmobiles, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Near the southern entrance, the road makes sharp changes of direction before descending through the forest to SR-14.

moments.title: Brian Head
moments.text: Brian Head rises north of Cedar Breaks in Dixie National Forest, reaching 11,312 feet. It is the highest peak on the Markagunt Plateau and in Iron County. A Forest Service lookout built in 1934–1935 stands on the summit, which has a road that can be driven in summer. This is a separate excursion beyond the monument: the peak lies outside its boundary, above the amphitheater rim.

moments.title: Alpine Pond
moments.text: At Alpine Pond, subalpine meadows occupy the canyon rim, reached by a trail from the road. The trailhead is at Chessman Ridge. Spring begins in June at this elevation, and wildflowers bloom through the short growing season. The monument’s plants include Colorado columbine, scarlet paintbrush and silvery lupin, alongside aspen, Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir.

moments.title: Cedar Breaks Visitor Center
moments.text: The historic rim cabin gives its logs unusually long ends, cut into tapering buttresses. A large stone chimney echoes their sloping shape, and projecting logs extend beneath a cedar-shake roof. The Civilian Conservation Corps built the two-room cabin in 1937 in the National Park Service Rustic style. It stands on the amphitheater rim overlooking the rock formations. A porch recessed into the front facade sits beneath its own inset shed roof at the entrance to the cabin. The same crew, from the Zion CCC camp, built the nearby caretaker’s cabin to a similar design.
moments.notice: Look for the tapered log ends and the stone chimney that echoes their shape.

practical: Cedar Breaks Visitor Center: The scenic road generally closes from mid-November through late May, becoming a groomed snowmobile, cross-country ski and snowshoe trail. Check road closures and openings before driving. (checked 2026-10-11)
